Summary: Rust 1.0 was released on May 15, 2015, marking the first stable version of the language. This release established Rust as a reliable systems programming language with a commitment to stability and backward compatibility. The milestone was celebrated with the release of version 1.87 on its 10th anniversary in 2025.

[1] Rust 2015 - The Rust Edition Guide
    https://doc.rust-lang.org/edition-guide/rust-2015/index.html
    # Rust 2015

Rust 2015 has a theme of “stability”. It commenced with the release of 1.0,
and is the “default edition”. The edition system was conceived in late 2017,
but Rust 1.0 was released in May of 2015. As such, 2015 is the edition
that you get when you don’t specify any particular edition, for backwards
compatibility reasons. [...] “Stability” is the theme of Rust 2015 because 1.0 marked a huge change in
Rust development. Previous to Rust 1.0, Rust was changing on a daily basis.
This made it very difficult to write large software in Rust, and made it
difficult to learn. With the release of Rust 1.0 and Rust 2015, we committed
to backwards compatibility, ensuring a solid foundation for people to build
projects on top of. [...] Since it’s the default edition, there’s no way to port your code to Rust
2015; it just is. You’ll be transitioning away from 2015, but never
really to 2015. As such, there’s not much else to say about it!

[...] | Written by Mike James |
| Saturday, 17 May 2025 |

    https://medium.com/@mattdark/rust-a-systems-programming-language-272ca761dfa0
    ## About

Rust is a systems programming language developed by the engineers of Mozilla. Rust could be categorized as a new language, as Rust 1.0, the first stable version was released on May 15th, 2015. The latest version today is Rust 1.20, that was released on August 31st, this year.

Rust is a compiled language like C or C++. [...] Rust is designed so that we can develop software where user interaction almost doesn’t exist. It’s excellent for applications within the client-server model or for internal tasks in our start-up or business. A daemon here or there.

By the way, two operating systems are being developed with this language.

Its syntax is similar to the one of C and C++. Let’s see some examples!

Let’s write the classic “Hello world!”!

Yep, we use semicolons and braces in this language [...] Similar to Python, Rust comes with its own package manager. This package manager is named Cargo and we can use it to create our projects, use third-party libraries, and so create our own libraries and register them.

It’s easy to contribute to the community.

The community of Rust is growing more and more, as more developers, projects and companies are betting for the language.

## Rust in our projects

Rust is designed to be integrated with projects that are in production.

Summary: Python 0.9.0 was first released in February 1991. It established the foundations of the language. Python has since evolved significantly.

[1] History and Evolution of Python Over Time
    https://www.luisllamas.es/en/history-evolution-python
    The first version of Python, known as Python 0.9.0, was released in February 1991. This version included many features that are still present in the language today, such as:

 Clear and readable syntax.
 Built-in data types like lists, dictionaries, and strings.
 Exception handling.
 Functions and modules.

Python 0.9.0 was a crucial starting point, as it established many of the foundations of the language as we know it today.

## Version Evolution

### Python 1.x (1994-2000) [...] Python 1.0 was released in January 1994. This version consolidated many of the features found in version 0.9.0 and introduced new functionalities, including:

 List comprehensions.
 Support for extension modules.

During the 1990s, Python grew in popularity, driven by its simplicity and flexibility. At this stage, Python became an attractive option for teaching programming and prototyping.

### Python 2.x (2000-2010) [...] Python 2.x continued to evolve with new versions throughout the decade, including Python 2.1, 2.2, 2.3, 2.4, 2.5, 2.6, and 2.7. This last version, Python 2.7, was released in July 2010 and was the last of the 2.x series, with extended support until 2020.

### Python 3.x (2008-Present)
